newsitem.title: USA: Clinton basks in lead, economy; Dole grounded.
newsitem.headline: Clinton basks in lead, economy; Dole grounded.

text.p: President Clinton, armed with more favourable polls and good economic news, took his re-election campaign to the heart of Republican territory Friday as stormy weather grounded his opponent Bob Dole.

The remnant of Hurrican Fran, which forced Dole to scrap a trip to New Jersey, capped a nightmare week for the challenger, who lost his two top media and advertising consultants Thursday in an internal power struggle.

Clinton meanwhile enjoyed the effects of an apparently successful exercise of military power against Iraq. Four polls issued Thursday put him between 11 to 17 percentage points ahead of Dole among likely voters, with Texan billionaire Ross Perot trailing with around 6 percent.

"The historical odds look strong for President Bill Clinton to be reelected to a second term ... A Dole win would require a dramatic shift in public opinion unprecedented since modern polling began," said Frank Newport of the Gallup polling organisation.

The Clinton campaign began airing a new television advertisement Friday attacking Dole on his proposed tax cut plan, the centrepiece of his campaign. The spot accused Dole of voting for tax hikes before he left the Senate and now proposing a "risky tax scheme" that would require cuts in Medicare health insurance for the elderly to help pay for it.
The president himself wrapped up a two-day swing through the Republican stronghold of Florida by stressing his record on the economy, education, the environment and health care.

"Let me assure you, we are not taking anyone or anyone's vote for granted," Clinton said in an address to delegates at the National Baptist Convention, an 8 million-member black organisation, in Orlando.

Florida has voted Republican in the past four presidential elections but polls show Clinton leading narrowly there now, boosted by support of senior citizens who fear losing their health insurance and other social benefits.
Clinton took credit for new unemployment figures that showed that the nation's jobless rate had dropped to 5.1 percent -- its lowest level in seven years.

"The American economy, my fellow Americans, is on the right track and we need to keep it going in that direction," said Clinton, who contends that the 15 percent income tax cut advocated by Dole would only reverse the economic progress.

The Dole campaign issued a six-page statement accusing Clinton of raising taxes and fees 127 times when he was governor of Arkansas, before he was elected president in 1992. And Republican Party chairman Haley Barbour issued a statement seizing on one poll showing Clinton only 11 points ahead, ignoring the other three in which his lead was 15-17 points.
In a statement, Barbour said the ABC/Washington Post poll proved voters were beginning to see through "Clinton's effort to co-opt Republican ideas and Republican policies."
Both the Clinton and Dole campaigns have now appointed negotiators to settle the details of the first presidential debate scheduled for Sept. 25. The two teams expect to start talks next week.
